title: Reading & Evaluating an Offer
summary: An offer letter's headline number is a marketing figure, not a forecast. Learn to decompose base, bonus, sign-on, and equity into their real mechanics and convert them into one comparable, risk-adjusted number.

slides.markdown:
Every offer letter leads with a **total compensation** figure designed to look as large as possible — it sums best-case bonus, undiscounted equity at grant-date value, and often a one-time sign-on bonus averaged into the headline. None of those assumptions survive contact with reality unchanged.

Reading an offer well means pulling apart four components — base, bonus, sign-on, and equity — understanding what each actually pays and when, then converting the whole package into a single risk-adjusted annualized number you can honestly compare against another offer or your current job.

This topic covers how to decompose an offer line by line, how vesting schedules quietly change what equity is actually worth, and the specific pitfall of comparing two offers' headline totals without adjusting for how much risk each number carries.

slides.sectionTitle: What each line of an offer actually means
slides.markdown:
- **Base salary**: fixed cash, paid every pay period regardless of company or individual performance. The only component that's fully guaranteed.
- **Bonus (target)**: a percentage of base, paid annually or semi-annually, scaled by company performance and your individual rating. "Target" means the number assumes both hit 100% — actual payout is usually a range around that, not a floor.
- **Sign-on bonus**: a one-time cash payment, often with a **clawback clause** requiring repayment (prorated) if you leave before 1-2 years — read this clause before counting the money as fully yours.
- **Equity**: RSUs (public companies) or options (private companies), granted at hire and vesting over time — worth zero until it vests, and its value floats with the stock price or the company's private valuation.

The biggest reading mistake is treating all four as equally certain cash. Only base is close to guaranteed; everything else carries a different kind of risk.

slides.sectionTitle: RSUs vs. stock options vs. private paper valuation
slides.markdown:
| | RSUs | Stock options | Private company equity |
|---|---|---|---|
| What you actually get | Shares outright at vest | The *right* to buy shares at a fixed strike price | Options or RSUs valued at the last funding round's price |
| When it has real value | Immediately at vest (public stock has a market price) | Only if stock price > strike price at exercise | Only if the company eventually IPOs, gets acquired, or has a liquidity event |
| Real risk | Stock price can still drop before you sell | Can go **underwater** (worthless) if price falls below strike | Illiquid; "valuation" is often a fiction until an actual exit |
| Tax timing | Taxed as income at vest | Taxed differently for ISOs vs NSOs, often at exercise | Depends on option type, often deferred until exit |

A private company quoting equity at "$400k over 4 years" is quoting a **paper number** against a valuation that may never be realized in cash — treat it as a lottery ticket with a real expected value, not as $100k/year of guaranteed comp.

slides.sectionTitle: A standard 4-year vesting schedule with a 1-year cliff
slides.subTitle: Diagram
slides.markdown:
The most common equity vesting shape at large tech companies: nothing vests for the first 12 months (the **cliff**), then 25% vests at the 1-year mark, and the remainder vests monthly or quarterly over the following 3 years.

![4-year vesting timeline with a 1-year cliff](assets/vesting-cliff-timeline.svg)

The cliff is the sharpest risk in the whole package: if you leave (or are let go) at month 11, you walk away with **zero** equity, regardless of how large the headline grant looked on your offer letter. This is also why some negotiations focus on a **sign-on bonus** structured to bridge exactly that first-year gap — it's cash that doesn't carry cliff risk.

slides.sectionTitle: Converting equity into a risk-adjusted annualized estimate
slides.markdown:
A rough, honest method: take the grant's headline value, divide by the vesting period in years to get a naive annual figure, then discount it for the specific risk category it falls into.

For public-company RSUs, the discount is small — mostly just stock price volatility, so a $200k/4-year grant is genuinely close to $50k/year, adjusted up or down with the stock. For private-company equity, apply a much steeper haircut — many candidates model it at 10-30% of headline value unless the company has a clear, near-term path to liquidity (a announced IPO date, a recent acquisition offer), since most startup equity never converts to real cash.

For options specifically, subtract the strike price from a realistic future share price estimate before annualizing — options priced above a plausible exit valuation are worth closer to zero than their headline count suggests, no matter how many shares are listed.

slides.sectionTitle: Two offers, same headline total, different risk profiles
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
| | Offer A: Big public tech co | Offer B: Series B startup |
|---|---|---|
| Headline total comp | $250k/year | $250k/year (incl. equity at last-round valuation) |
| Base salary | $175k | $150k |
| Bonus | $20k target, historically paid ~95% | No bonus program |
| Equity value | $55k/year RSUs, liquid, low volatility | $100k/year in options, illiquid, 0% chance of value unless there's an exit |
| Realistic risk-adjusted total | ~$240k | ~$175-190k (options haircut applied) |

Both offers show "$250k" on the letter. Only one of them is actually close to that in expected value. Neither is objectively wrong to take — the startup might also come with faster scope growth or a mission you care about — but comparing the two headline numbers as if they were equally real is the mistake, not the choice itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Comparing headline totals without adjusting for vesting and risk
slides.subTitle: Pitfall
slides.markdown:
The single most common evaluation mistake: putting two offer letters side by side and comparing the top-line "total compensation" number, without checking whether both use the same assumptions.

This fails in both directions. It can make a risky private-company offer look equal to a safe public one (ignoring that most of the private number is a lottery ticket), and it can also make an offer with a large **sign-on bonus** look better than it is over multiple years, since a one-time bonus inflates year-one total but contributes nothing to years two through four.

A reliable habit: build a simple per-year table for each offer — base, actual expected bonus, sign-on only in the year it's paid, and equity divided by its real vesting schedule — before comparing any single "total comp" figure across offers.

A $30k sign-on bonus is genuinely attractive cash, but almost every sign-on comes with a **clawback clause**: if you leave before a set period (commonly 12-24 months), you owe back a prorated portion — sometimes the full amount, sometimes scaled by months remaining.

This matters for two reasons interviewers and offer-readers routinely miss. First, it changes the real risk of leaving early: a candidate weighing an exit at month 8 needs to know they'd owe back roughly two-thirds of the bonus, not just forfeit unvested equity. Second, some companies use a large sign-on specifically to **backfill a first-year equity cliff gap** — in which case it isn't a bonus so much as the company's way of paying you for the year you'd otherwise get zero equity.

Always read the clawback clause's exact repayment schedule before treating a sign-on number as free money.

slides.sectionTitle: Refresher grants and why year-one equity isn't the whole story
slides.markdown:
Most public tech companies grant additional **refresher equity** annually on top of the initial grant, typically tied to performance review results. This matters for comparing offers because a company with a strong, predictable refresher culture can make a lower initial grant perform better over 4+ years than a larger one-time grant with weak refreshers.

Ask directly (a normal, expected question): "what does refresher equity typically look like for someone performing well at this level?" A vague or evasive answer is itself informative — companies with a genuinely strong refresher program are usually happy to describe it in general terms, since it's a retention selling point for them too.

The senior-level nuance: initial grant size gets most of a candidate's attention because it's the biggest number on the offer letter, but refresher policy is often the bigger long-term driver of total comp past year two.

slides.subTitle: Concrete example
slides.markdown:
```
Offer: base $160k, bonus target 15%, sign-on $20k (2-yr clawback),
equity $160k over 4 years (public company RSUs), starting this year.

Year 1: base 160k + bonus (est. 95% of target = 14.25k) + sign-on 20k
        + equity vested this year (0, due to 1-yr cliff) = $194.25k
Year 2: base 160k + bonus 14.25k + equity (25% cliff vest + partial
        year-2 monthly vest, roughly 30k of the 4-yr grant) = $204.25k
Year 3: base 160k + bonus 14.25k + equity (~40k/yr steady-state) = $214.25k

Naive headline math ($160k + 24k bonus + 40k equity/yr) would have
claimed ~$224k in year 1 — the cliff alone makes that off by $30k.
```

The cliff, not the equity size, is what makes year one look meaningfully weaker than the naive average — a detail the offer letter's "total comp: $224k" line never surfaces on its own.

Once you've decomposed an offer into a risk-adjusted, year-by-year picture, you know exactly which lever is weakest and worth pushing on — maybe the equity is solid but the base is below band, or the sign-on doesn't actually cover the cliff gap you're worried about.

[Understanding levels and comp bands](levels-comp-bands) covers how the level underneath this offer sets its ceiling in the first place, and negotiation tactics and scripts covers exactly how to phrase a counter once you know which number to push.
